headline: New Haven Rockpiles: Porgies by the Dozen, Sea Bass Riding Shotgun
subhead: Full moon current sharpens the bottom bite on the breakwalls while stripers slide onto the Charles Island bar after dark.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, top of the flood, I dropped a size 4 hi-lo rig dressed with squid strips off the New Haven Outer Breakwall and the sinker never got a chance to sit still. Porgies came up two at a time — 12 to 15 inches, fat as dinner plates, and mad about it. That's the kind of start that tells you the whole day's going to go right, and for once it actually did.

The breakwalls have been the story all week. Both the Outer and the West Wall are holding thick porgy numbers in 18 to 22 feet, best on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing — basically anytime there's current moving but the wind hasn't kicked up a chop to push you off the spot. Clam is still king for bait, but I've been running a two-hook bottom rig with green crab on the top hook and squid on the bottom just to see which the porgies want more on a given tide, and honestly they don't care — they're eating everything down there right now. Mixed into that same structure are black sea bass, and not the dink humpbacks we were pulling in June. Guys working small strips of squid on 1/2-ounce jigheads, bounced right off the riprap, are finding keepers in the 14 to 17-inch range, some pushing 3 pounds. The sea bass want the deeper pockets between the rock piles, not the shallow lip, so if you're marking fish on the sounder but not connecting, slide out ten feet toward the channel side of the wall.

Falkner Island is fishing the same way but bigger. That reef structure off the island in 35 to 40 feet has been holding a better class of sea bass — diamond jigs tipped with squid strips, dropped straight down and worked with short hops off bottom, have been the ticket on the last hour of the ebb when the current lightens up enough to actually feel your jig. It's a run-and-gun spot; you might mark fish thick on one drift and get nothing the next, so I keep making short drifts and marking waypoints rather than anchoring up and hoping.

Blackfish are stacked on both the breakwalls and the Falkner rockpiles right now, which is a little bit of a tease since the season's closed for the summer stretch. Green crab drops on light tackle are producing plenty of catch-and-release action — 18 to 22-inch tog thumping the rod tip and peeling drag off spinning gear you'd normally use for porgies. It's fun, it's free, and it's a good preview of what October's going to look like once the season flips back open.

Stripers are a different animal entirely with the water running warm — Kings Point read 72.5 this week and the harbor itself has felt every bit that warm on the surface, so the bass have gone strictly low-light on us. Charles Island and that sandbar connecting it to Silver Sands are still the best bet, but you want to be there for last light into full dark on the building tide, not midday. Bunker chunks fished tight to the bar edge where the current sweeps around the point have been drawing strikes from schoolies up through 28-inch fish. A few guys working white paddletails on the drift over the bar right at dusk have connected too, but the chunk bite has been more consistent. Daytime, forget it — the fish are sitting deep and sulking until the sun drops.

Bluefish have been the pleasant surprise. We flagged the peanut bunker push a couple weeks back and said the cocktail blues would follow them into the back bays, and that's exactly what's showing up now — snapper-sized blues mixed with cocktail fish in the 2 to 4-pound range, working pods of peanuts right at the mouth of New Haven Harbor on the outgoing tide. Small metal, half-ounce Deadly Dicks or similar, cast into the boils has been about as simple as fishing gets this week.

Fluke are still around but you have to work for them. Milford Gulf and the channel edges off Welch's Point have given up a scattered pick of keepers — 18 to 22 inches — on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow through the deeper cuts on the last of the outgoing. It's not a banner fluke year in this stretch, and I won't pretend otherwise. You might make three drifts and get one fish, but that one fish has been a legitimate keeper more often than not, which counts for something.

This week's full moon has put some real muscle into the tides, and that's been the difference-maker on the bottom bite — more current means more bait getting pushed off the rocks, means more porgies and sea bass stacked up feeding on it. That current strength should hold through the weekend before easing back into a more standard push by midweek. If I had one trip to make, I'd hit the Outer Breakwall on the last two hours of an incoming tide for porgies and sea bass, then swing by Charles Island right at dusk with a bag of bunker chunks and see if the stripers want to cooperate. Bring both rigs — this time of year, the bite can flip on you fast depending on which way the light's going.
